newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper says U.S. "demonizes" Colombia.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper says U.S. "demonizes" Colombia.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper accused Washington on Tuesday of "demonizing" Colombia and said the U.S. drug certification process that blacklists countries deemed untrustworthy in the drugs fight fostered "confrontation and not cooperation" in the war against drugs.
"Certification is an unacceptable mechanism of unilateral pressure ... which puts relations between countries on the grounds of confrontation and not cooperation," Samper said.
"It exacerbates nationalistic sentiments, demoralises government officials and demonises the institutions of a solid and serious democracy in the eyes of the world in an unfair way," he added.

Colombia was severely shaken last March when President Bill Clinton included it on a list of states -- Afghanistan, Burma, Iran, Nigeria and Syria -- that had failed to cooperate fully in global anti-drug efforts.

In an annual report required by Congress, Clinton will announce this week whether Colombia should remain on the list or be "certified" as a trustworthy ally in the drug fight. A second consecutive decertification would trigger economic sanctions that Clinton fell short of imposing in 1996.
Samper spoke at a ceremony in which he formally sanctioned a law, passed by Colombia's Congress last week, that dramatically increased penalties for drug trafficking.
He did not say how Colombia would react if it were decertified again and hit with commercial sanctions, such as the loss of tariff preferences enjoyed by Colombian exporters.

But Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia told reporters such a move would be "a disincentive to continue the hard work that's left to us on the drugs front." Hinting at a possible crackdown on covert U.S. anti-drug operations on Colombian soil, she added that decertification "would imply a revision of the mechanisms of cooperation" with Washington.
In his speech, Samper said the law approved last week was just one of many steps Colombia had taken over the past year to stem the flow of cocaine and heroin onto U.S. streets.

Apart from passing an aggressive asset forfeiture law allowing for the seizure of proceeds from the drug trade, he said Colombia's counter-narcotics programme -- which cost the country $1.3 billion in 1996 -- featured one of the world's most ambitious drug crop eradication programmes.

He also stressed that dozens of Colombian soliders, police and civilians had died on the frontlines of the drug war last year and said only 10 percent of the financial costs of the war was covered by foreign assistance.
"We have concrete facts to show the world in response to the negative rhetoric of those now trying to disqualify results of the war Colombia is waging against drug trafficking," Samper said.

U.S. officials say that under Samper's presidency Colombia, which was already the world's leading supplier of cocaine, has become a growing source of coca leaf -- the raw material for the drug -- and a leading supplier of heroin.

In testimony to Congress earlier this month, Asssistant Secretary of State Robert Gelbard also said that Samper had failed to shake off allegations that he knowingly received millions of dollars in Cali cartel drug money to finance his 1994 election campaign.

Samper was absolved by Congress last year of any wrongdoing in connection with his campaign finances. But Gelbard called him "a truly corrupt president who has had a clear history of cooperating with drug dealers and receiving drug money back to 1982."
